DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
## Summary

Raising the weekend rate to £165 is plausible. It would match the cheapest hotel in the competitive set, and occupancy could fall by about 10 points before room revenue declines. But the evidence the proposal offers for it doesn't hold:
- the price-sensitivity "test" is a seasonal effect;
- the £204,000 uses the wrong room count;
- the two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday segment.

£204,000 is not a floor. The figure is overstated, and the part the author calls unquantified upside could turn out to be a loss.

## What I checked

These figures are correct:
- **Average occupancy:** the twelve monthly figures average 79.2%, which matches the stated 79%.
- **Competitor gap:** £145 against competitors at £165–180 is a gap of £20–35.
- **Weekend nights:** 52 × 2 = 104 a year.

## Errors

**1. The room count is wrong.** Section 2 says Harbourside has 112 rooms. Section 5 uses 124. The £204,000 only works with 124: 124 × 104 × 0.79 × £20 = £203,757. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives **£184,000**.

**2. The price "test" is seasonal, not a response to price.** Table 1 shows July and August are the strongest months every year because of the harbour festival and school holidays, as section 2 itself says. A rise from 81% in June to 89% in July is what the season produces regardless of the rate.

Booking lead times make the test weaker still. The rise took effect in the last week of June. Many July guests, especially for the festival, will have booked weeks or months earlier at £135, so July occupancy says little about demand at £145.

Better evidence already exists in the hotel's own data:
- **2024 against 2025:** compare July–December occupancy in each year, at £135 and £145 respectively. 2024 isn't in the paper, but the hotel will have it.
- **Booking pace:** check whether pick-up slowed for bookings made after the rise compared with before it.

**3. The two-night minimum conflicts with wedding guests.** Section 4 says weddings at Quayside Hall account for about 38% of Saturday room bookings. Those guests arrive on the Saturday and leave on the Sunday, which is exactly the single-night stay the minimum would block. Contracts already signed are honoured, but future wedding blocks and individual wedding guests would face a two-night requirement or book elsewhere.

**4. The two-night minimum can lose revenue as well as add it.** The hotel sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. On the other 21 Saturdays, rooms were empty, and a two-night minimum turns away single-night guests who would have filled them. The author describes the unquantified effect as pure upside, making £204,000 "a floor." But the effect could be negative, especially in the shoulder months the paper expects to benefit most. Hotels normally apply minimum stays only on dates expected to sell out.

**5. Not every weekend room is sold at BAR.** The £20 is applied to every occupied weekend room, but the rise only affects rooms sold at the Best Available Rate. It does not apply to:
- corporate contracted rates;
- group rates, which may include the wedding blocks;
- packages.

Two further deductions probably apply:
- **VAT.** UK room rates are normally quoted including 20% VAT, so £20 on the rate is about £16.67 of net room revenue.
- **Online travel agent commission.** This takes a further share of each booking made through those channels.

The realistic figure is:

> 112 × 104 × occupancy × share of weekend rooms sold at BAR × £16.67, minus commission

For illustration only: if 60% of weekend room nights are sold at BAR, the net figure is roughly £90,000–95,000 before commission. The actual BAR share is available from the property management system.

## Claims that are not evidenced

- **Value for money.** The 8.4 score was measured at the lower rate, from guests who chose to book. It doesn't show how guests would rate the hotel at £165.
- **"Prudent."** Calling the no-change occupancy assumption prudent rests on the flawed test in point 2. Prudent would mean modelling a range.
- **First-year revenue.** Bookings already made for June onward at £145 will reduce first-year revenue below any annual figure.

## Break-even

Ignoring mix and commission, weekend room revenue per available room is £145 × 79% = £114.55 now. At £165, occupancy would have to fall below **69.4%**, a drop of about 10 points, before that revenue falls. This is the strongest argument for the rate rise, and the paper doesn't make it. Weekend guests also spend on food, drink and other services, so lost occupancy costs more than room revenue alone.

## Monitoring

The five-point trigger sits within the break-even margin, which is reasonable. Two weaknesses:
- **Detection is slower than "within a month."** Occupancy is reviewed monthly and measured after the month ends. By then later months are already partly booked. A trigger on weekly booking pace would detect a problem sooner.
- **Compare against 2024 as well as 2025.** Normal variation from one year to the next can be several points. Comparing against both years helps separate a pricing effect from ordinary variation.

## Settled and open

**Settled:**
- the room count error;
- the June-to-July "test" not measuring price sensitivity;
- the conflict between the minimum stay and wedding guests.

**Likely, and quick to confirm:**
- the VAT and BAR-mix effects. The accounts and the property management system will confirm both.

**Open:**
- how sensitive weekend demand is to price. A 2024–2025 comparison and booking-pace data will give a first answer, and monitoring after launch will refine it.
- the net effect of the two-night minimum. Applying it on a few high-demand dates first and measuring the result would settle this.

## Recommendation

**Rate rise:**
- Approve the £165 rate. Base the case on the competitor gap and the roughly 10-point break-even margin, not on the June test.
- Restate the projection with 112 rooms, the actual BAR share, and figures net of VAT and commission.

**Two-night minimum:**
- Do not approve it as drafted.
- Apply it only to Saturdays forecast to sell out.
- Exempt wedding and group blocks.
- Review it after one season.
